summary: Betrayed by his stepfather Ganelon, Roland dies with the rear guard at Roncevaux rather than call for help, and Charlemagne avenges him on the Saracens and the traitor.

hunger.why: No character seeks or enjoys food.

thirst.why: No character seeks water, though Roland dies by a stream.

feeling-cold-hot.why: No extreme heat or cold threatens anyone.

sleepiness.why: Charlemagne's prophetic dreams come to him in sleep, but fatigue is not a concern.

curiosity.why: No one explores unfamiliar places; the army crosses known passes.

explanation-seeking.why: Charlemagne's dreams foreshadow treachery, but no mystery is investigated.

skill-acquisition.why: The knights are already masters; no one trains or improves.

resource-accumulation.why: Marsile bribes Ganelon with gold and offers Charlemagne treasure; wealth is a tool of treachery, not a goal.

resource-foraging.why: No one searches for scarce resources.

mental-time-travel.why: Ganelon plots the ambush and Charlemagne's dreams foretell the future, but planning is brief.

fear-of-predators.why: A bear and a leopard attack Charlemagne in his dream; animals threaten no one awake.

fear-of-aggressors.why: The Saracen ambush at Roncevaux, wave after wave against the rear guard, then Charlemagne's battles with Marsile and Baligant, fill the poem.

fear-of-heights.why: The Pyrenean passes are high, but no one risks a fall.

disgust.why: No rot, disease, or contamination threatens a character.

pain-aversion.why: Blow by blow the poem records split helmets and bodies, Oliver's death wound, and Roland bursting his temple blowing the oliphant.

pride.why: Roland's prowess is proclaimed on every side, and his refusal to sound the horn rests on confidence in his own excellence.

shame.why: Roland will not blow the horn because no one shall sing that he called for help out of fear; dread of disgrace seals his fate.

moral-pride.why: Roland and the peers die for Charlemagne and Christendom rather than yield, and Thierry fights Pinabel to uphold the right.

guilt.why: Roland grieves over the dead peers but never truly blames himself; Oliver's reproach stands in for guilt.

warmth.why: Roland carries the bodies of the peers to Turpin and weeps over them, and Turpin blesses the dying.

moral-blame.why: Ganelon's treason is condemned and tried before Charlemagne, with Thierry's victory proving his guilt.

moral-praise.why: Angels bear Roland's soul to heaven and the poem celebrates him as a martyr of the faith.

revenge.why: Ganelon betrays Roland to pay him back, and Charlemagne destroys the Saracens and has Ganelon torn apart to avenge the rear guard.

forgiveness.why: Roland forgives Oliver when the blinded Oliver strikes him; otherwise there is no reconciliation.

compassion.why: Roland weeps for his men and Charlemagne laments over the dead, but pity for the weak is not a motive.

friendship.why: Roland and Oliver, the twelve peers, fight and die side by side; their companionship anchors the battle.

sadness.why: Charlemagne's lament over Roland's body and Aude's death at the news are extended scenes of grief.

humor.why: There is no humor in the poem.

reasoning.why: The council debates Marsile's offer, Roland and Oliver argue about the horn, and the trial of Ganelon is argued before the barons.

coalitional-affiliation.why: Christians against pagans, Franks against Saracens: the poem states that pagans are wrong and Christians are right, and loyalty to the group is absolute.

status-seeking.why: Roland's renown and his place as Charlemagne's champion are at stake, though pride expresses it more than ambition.

envy.why: Ganelon resents Roland's favor and wealth, a seed of the betrayal.

anger.why: Ganelon's fury at being named envoy, Roland's battle rage, and Charlemagne's wrath against the Saracens drive the action.

hatred.why: Ganelon hates Roland enough to sell him to the enemy, and Christians and Saracens exult in each other's deaths.

romantic-affiliation.why: Aude is Roland's betrothed, mentioned briefly.

long-term-love.why: Aude dies on hearing of Roland's death, a single scene of devoted commitment.

familial-love.why: Ganelon is Roland's stepfather, Charlemagne loves Roland as his nephew, and Aude is Oliver's sister; kinship frames the betrayal.
